context_blurb:
Everything, from a gold ring to the air you breathe, is made of particles, tiny pieces far too small to see. Whether something is a solid, a liquid or a gas depends on how tightly its particles are packed and how fast they move. That one idea explains why ice holds its shape, why water pours and why a mirror fogs up.

In a solid, the particles are packed tightly and held in fixed places, like students squeezed into a crowded class photo: nobody can swap places, but everybody fidgets. That is why ice keeps its shape. Yet the particles are never still, not even in the cold of a freezer: each one vibrates, shaking back and forth on its own spot, packed close against its neighbours.

In a liquid, the particles stay close together, so the liquid keeps its volume, the amount of room it takes up. A liquid's particles stay close but slide past one another all the time, so the liquid flows into the shape of whatever holds it.

In a gas, the particles are far apart, and they move fast and freely in all directions. Each one zooms in a straight line until it hits another particle or a wall, then bounces off. Nothing holds gas particles together, so their own motion carries them into every corner of any container. They do not shove one another apart from a distance; they meet only when they bump into each other.

Because gas particles are so far apart, most of a gas is empty space. Air's particles are far apart, with empty space all around them, so squeezing air pushes them closer together. A diver's tank holds only about eleven litres of water, yet a pump can force some two thousand three hundred litres of air into it, and that air is still a gas. Water can hardly be squeezed at all, because its particles already touch. Try it with a plastic syringe: block the tip, and the plunger pushes a long way into trapped air but hardly moves against trapped water.

Heating gives particles more energy, so they move faster; cooling slows them down. In a jeweller's furnace, the particles of a gold ring vibrate harder and harder. At the melting point, the temperature where a solid turns to liquid, the gold's particles have enough energy to break free of their fixed places. No particle melts or goes soft; only the way the particles are held together changes.

Heat a flask of water and its particles speed up too. At the boiling point, particles all through the water gain enough energy to pull away from one another. They gather into bubbles of water vapour, which is water in the form of a gas, and the bubbles rise and escape. Many people guess those bubbles are hydrogen and oxygen, but every particle that leaves is still a whole water particle.

The water particles in ice, in liquid water and in vapour are the very same ones, and the size of each particle never changes. What changes is how fast they move and how strongly they hold on to one another. When a heated thing swells, it is the space between its particles that grows.

Cooling runs the story backwards. After a hot shower, the air is full of water vapour. When the vapour touches the cool mirror, the glass takes energy from it, so its particles slow down and come close together, clinging to one another as a liquid. That change, a gas turning into a liquid, is called condensation: the reverse of evaporation.
